title: Compound interest: money that grows on money
heading: Summary
text: With compound interest, you earn interest on your savings and on the interest you already earned.

title: Compound interest: money that grows on money
heading: Overview
text: When you keep money in a savings account, the bank pays you a small extra amount for holding it. That extra amount is called interest. You can think of it as a thank-you from the bank.

title: Compound interest: money that grows on money
heading: Simple interest first
text: Say you put one hundred dollars in an account that pays five percent each year. After one year, you earn five dollars. If the bank only ever paid interest on your first hundred dollars, you would earn five dollars every year. After two years you would have one hundred ten dollars.

title: Compound interest: money that grows on money
heading: Where compounding comes in
text:
Most savings accounts work a little differently. In year two, the bank pays interest on your whole balance, including the five dollars you already earned. That is compound interest.

- Start: $100.00
- After year 1: $105.00
- After year 2: $110.25

That extra twenty-five cents does not look like much. It came from interest earning its own interest. Over many years, the gap gets bigger, because each year's growth is built on a larger pile.

title: Compound interest: money that grows on money
heading: Time is the secret ingredient
text:
The longer money stays in the account, the more time it has to compound. Starting early can matter more than starting big. Someone who saves a small amount for many years can end up with more than someone who saves a larger amount for only a short time.

Rates change, and the numbers here are only examples. Always check the rate that an account really pays.

title: Compound interest: money that grows on money
heading: Try it
text: Use a compound interest calculator. The one on Investor.gov is a good place to start. Enter one hundred dollars and a rate of five percent. Compare ten years with twenty years, and notice how much the second ten years adds.

title: Drop by drop: how small habits fill a big jar
heading: Summary
text: Small amounts, added again and again, can grow into something big.

title: Drop by drop: how small habits fill a big jar
heading: Overview
text: There is an old saying that water drops, one at a time, can fill a very large jar. One drop looks like nothing. But the drops keep coming, and over time the jar fills up.

title: Drop by drop: how small habits fill a big jar
heading: Money works the same way
text:
Saving one dollar does not feel like much. It will not buy a bike or a game. But if you save one dollar every week, that is fifty-two dollars in a year. Add a little more when you can, and the jar fills faster.

The important part is not the size of each drop. It is that the drops keep coming. A small amount saved every week often beats a big amount saved once and then forgotten.

title: Drop by drop: how small habits fill a big jar
heading: Habits make it easy
text: When you save at the same time every week, such as the day you get your allowance, you stop having to decide each time. It becomes part of your routine, like brushing your teeth. Habits take the effort out of doing the right thing.

title: Drop by drop: how small habits fill a big jar
heading: It works the other way too
text: Small spending drops add up as well. A snack here and a sticker there may feel tiny, but together they can empty a jar without you noticing. This is not a reason to feel bad about spending. It is a reason to notice, so you can spend on purpose.

title: Drop by drop: how small habits fill a big jar
heading: Patience is part of the plan
text: Some weeks, the jar will look almost the same. Keep going. Slow growth is still growth, and each week that you keep the habit, you get better at it.

title: Drop by drop: how small habits fill a big jar
heading: Try it
text: Pick a small amount you can save every week without it feeling hard. Choose a day, and put it in your jar at the same time each week. After four weeks, count your drops and see how much you have.

title: Money talks at home: learning together
heading: Summary
text: Families learn more about money when they talk about it together.

title: Money talks at home: learning together
heading: Overview
text: Money is something every family deals with. Many families do not talk about it much, but talking about money together can help everyone learn.

title: Money talks at home: learning together
heading: Why talk about money?
text: You learn many things from the people around you. If you see an adult compare prices, make a budget, or wait before buying something, you pick up that habit too. When you ask questions, adults can share what they have learned, including their own mistakes. Everyone in a family can learn from each other, grown-ups included.

title: Money talks at home: learning together
heading: What can a family talk about?
text:
You do not need to share private details, like how much money a person has. Grown-ups decide what to share. There are plenty of easy topics to start with.

- How do you decide what is a need and what is a want?
- What is something our family is saving for together?
- What is one money lesson you learned when you were young?
- What is a good way to share or give to others?

title: Money talks at home: learning together
heading: Small steps, shared goals
text: A family can pick a goal together, like a trip or a special dinner, and each person can add their own drops. Everyone's effort counts, whether it is a big amount or a small one. When each person learns to handle money wisely, the whole family becomes more prepared, and more generous too.

title: Money talks at home: learning together
heading: Be kind and curious
text: Money can feel stressful for some families. If a question feels hard, it is okay to pause and come back to it later. The goal is to learn together, not to judge anyone.

title: Money talks at home: learning together
heading: Try it
text: Pick one question from the list and ask someone in your family at dinner this week. Listen to their answer, then share yours. Write down one new idea you heard.

title: Needs and wants: spending on purpose
heading: Summary
text: A need is something you must have. A want is something that would be nice to have.

title: Needs and wants: spending on purpose
heading: Overview
text: Every day, people make choices about money. One of the best habits you can build is to ask a simple question first: is this a need or a want?

title: Needs and wants: spending on purpose
heading: What is a need?
text: A need is something you must have to stay healthy and safe. Food, a place to live, clothes for the weather, and medicine are needs. You cannot go without them.

title: Needs and wants: spending on purpose
heading: What is a want?
text: A want is something that would be nice to have, but you can live without it. A new video game, a second pair of fancy shoes, or a snack at the mall are wants. Wants are not bad. They make life fun. The trick is to choose them on purpose.

title: Needs and wants: spending on purpose
heading: Some things are in the middle
text: Sometimes the line is blurry. You need shoes, but you may not need the most expensive pair. You need to eat, but you do not need a meal at a restaurant. When a need has a cheaper choice and a fancier choice, the cheaper one already covers the need. The extra money you pay for the fancy one is the want part.

title: Needs and wants: spending on purpose
heading: Trade-offs
text: Money is limited, so choosing one thing often means giving up another. This is called a trade-off. If you spend ten dollars on a toy today, you cannot also put that ten dollars toward your bike fund. Neither choice is always right. What matters is that you notice the trade-off before you spend.

title: Needs and wants: spending on purpose
heading: Try it
text: Look at the last three things you bought or asked for. Label each one as a need or a want. Then pick one want you could wait on for a week. When the week is over, ask yourself if you still want it just as much.

title: Your piggy bank: where saving starts
heading: Summary
text: A piggy bank is a safe place to keep money you do not spend today.

title: Your piggy bank: where saving starts
heading: Overview
text: A piggy bank is a simple tool with a big job. It keeps your money safe so you can use it later.

title: Your piggy bank: where saving starts
heading: Why save?
text: When you get money, you have a choice. You can spend it now, or you can save some for later. Saving means keeping money instead of spending it right away. Saved money can help you buy something bigger, like a game or a bike, that you could not afford with just one allowance.

title: Your piggy bank: where saving starts
heading: How a piggy bank works
text:
Every time you put money in, it is called a deposit. Your pile grows a little at a time, and small deposits add up. If you put in five dollars a week, you will have twenty dollars after four weeks. After twelve weeks, you will have sixty dollars.

A piggy bank also gives you a pause. Because your money is tucked away, you have to stop and think before you take it out. That pause helps you avoid spending on things you will forget about next week.

title: Your piggy bank: where saving starts
heading: Saving with a goal
text:
Saving is easier when you know what you are saving for. A goal is something you want to reach. Pick your goal and find out its price. Then divide the price by the number of weeks you are willing to wait.

Say a game costs forty dollars and you want it in eight weeks. Forty divided by eight is five, so you need to save five dollars each week. If you save a little more some weeks, you will get there even sooner.

title: Your piggy bank: where saving starts
heading: What if you slip?
text: Everyone spends some of their savings by accident sometimes. That is okay. Look at your goal again, work out the new weekly amount, and keep going. A small setback does not cancel your plan.

title: Your piggy bank: where saving starts
heading: Try it
text: Pick one thing you really want. Write down its price. Decide how many weeks you can wait, and work out how much to save each week. Then make your first deposit today, even if it is only a little.

title: What are taxes?
heading: Summary
text: Taxes are money that people and businesses pay to the government to fund shared services.

title: What are taxes?
heading: Overview
text: Taxes are money that people and businesses pay to the government. The government uses that money to pay for things that everyone shares.

title: What are taxes?
heading: What do taxes pay for?
text: Think about the things you use every day that you do not pay for at the door. Public schools, roads and bridges, parks, libraries, fire trucks, and police all depend on tax money. Taxes also help pay for people who are sick or out of work, and for keeping the country safe.

title: What are taxes?
heading: Who pays taxes?
text:
Most adults pay taxes, and so do businesses. There are a few main kinds.

- **Income tax:** a part of the money you earn from a job.
- **Sales tax:** a small amount added when you buy something in a store.
- **Property tax:** money paid by people who own land or buildings, which often helps pay for local schools.

You may have seen sales tax already. If a toy has a ten dollar price tag, the total at the register can be a bit higher because of the tax.

title: What are taxes?
heading: Why do taxes matter to you?
text:
When you get your first paycheck, it may be smaller than you expected. That is because some of the money was already sent to the government as tax. Knowing this ahead of time helps you plan how much you will really have to spend and save.

Tax rules differ from place to place and change over time. This article is for learning and is not tax advice.

title: What are taxes?
heading: Try it
text: Look at a receipt from a store and find the line that says tax. Work out how much extra you paid compared to the price tags. Then list three things in your town that taxes help pay for.

title: What is a stock?
heading: Summary
text: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a company.

title: What is a stock?
heading: Overview
text: A stock is a tiny slice of ownership in a company. If a company were a pizza, a stock would be one slice. People who own stock are called shareholders, and each slice is called a share.

title: What is a stock?
heading: Why do companies sell stock?
text: Building a business takes money. A company might need money to open stores, build products, or hire workers. One way to raise money is to sell shares to the public. The company gets cash to grow, and the buyers get a small piece of the company.

title: What is a stock?
heading: How do shareholders make money?
text:
There are two main ways.

- **The price goes up.** If you buy a share and later sell it for more than you paid, you keep the difference.
- **Dividends.** Some companies share part of their profits with their shareholders. That payment is called a dividend.

title: What is a stock?
heading: Prices can fall too
text: A share price can go down as well as up. If the company does poorly, or people lose faith in it, the price can drop, and you could get back less than you paid. This is why stocks are called risky. Nobody can know ahead of time which way a price will move.

title: What is a stock?
heading: Where are stocks bought and sold?
text:
Shares trade on a stock market. That is a place, often online, where buyers and sellers meet. The price of a share changes during the day as people buy and sell.

This article is for learning. It is not advice about what to buy.

title: What is a stock?
heading: Try it
text: Pick a company you know, like a game maker or a snack brand. Find out whether it sells stock to the public. If it does, look up its share price today and again in a week. Write down whether it moved, and one reason why it might have.
